_meta.source: Augustine on Genesis — seed corpus shipped with γ.3 (2026-05-11).
_meta.scope: Curated interpretive summaries verse-keyed to Genesis 1-3. Each entry is a paraphrased summary of the Church Father's argument, NOT a verbatim quote — verbatim passages from the NPNF text dump will land in a future γ.3.x once that ETL ships.
_meta.public_domain_basis: Augustine d. 430 AD; Schaff/Dods translations published 1880s-1900s, all out of copyright in every jurisdiction.

entries.work: De Genesi ad litteram (The Literal Meaning of Genesis)
entries.summary: Augustine reads 'In the beginning' (in principio) as referring not merely to a temporal first moment but to the eternal Word (Christ) in whom all things are made. Creation, on this account, is the Father speaking the Word — heaven and earth proceed from the Trinitarian relations rather than from raw temporal succession.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, Bk I. NPNF Series 1, vol. 4, ed. Schaff. PD.

entries.summary: On 'the earth was formless and void', Augustine identifies the prima materia — formless matter — as itself created ex nihilo, not co-eternal with God. The 'Spirit moving over the waters' is the Holy Spirit, whose hovering is a figure for the divine love bestowing form on the formless.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, Bk I.4. NPNF Series 1, vol. 4. PD.

entries.summary: 'Let there be light' is God's first spoken act in Augustine's reading: not the creation of physical sun-light (that comes on day four) but the establishment of intellectual or spiritual light — the rational creation, the angels, illumined by the Word. Physical light follows as a temporal echo of the spiritual original.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, Bk I.9. NPNF Series 1, vol. 4. PD.

entries.summary: 'Let us make man in our image' — the plural 'us' is, for Augustine, the Trinitarian council, the Father addressing the Son and the Spirit. The 'image' is properly located in the rational soul (mens), not the body; specifically in its capacity for memory, understanding, and will — a created analogue of the Trinitarian processions.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Trinitate, Bk XII.7 + De Genesi ad litteram VI.12. NPNF Series 1, vols. 3 + 4. PD.

entries.summary: On God breathing into Adam, Augustine resists a crudely material reading: the 'breath of life' is the rational soul, infused directly by God (not propagated from prior material). The body is formed from earth as a vessel; the soul is the direct image of God within the human composite.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram, Bk VII.1-3. NPNF Series 1, vol. 4. PD.

entries.work: De Genesi contra Manichaeos (Two Books on Genesis Against the Manichees)
entries.summary: Against the Manichaean reading that finds the serpent to be an inherently-evil being, Augustine insists the serpent is a created good twisted by Satan's prior fall. The 'subtlety' is morally neutral as creature-attribute; only its use under the devil's influence makes it the vehicle of temptation.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De Genesi contra Manichaeos, Bk II.14. NPNF Series 1, vol. 4. PD.

entries.work: De civitate Dei (The City of God)
entries.summary: The Fall, for Augustine, is fundamentally a *will-fault* (defectus voluntatis) before it is an act: Eve and Adam consent inwardly to the serpent's lie before any fruit is eaten. The eating is the visible expression of an interior turning away from God; original sin is therefore primarily a disordered love, not merely a transgressive deed.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De civitate Dei, Bk XIV.13. NPNF Series 1, vol. 2. PD.

entries.summary: The protoevangelium ('he shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel') is read Christologically: the woman's seed is Christ; the bruised heel is the Cross; the crushed head is the definitive defeat of the devil. This is the first announcement of redemption in the Genesis narrative — the Christian reading of the OT begins here.
entries.attribution: Augustine, De civitate Dei, Bk XVI.27. NPNF Series 1, vol. 2. PD.
